# Temperare documentation map

Temperare checks code against the rules a repository has chosen to enforce, and reports what it finds. It is a
command-line program, `temperare`, short name `tm`. It runs clippy, SwiftLint, ruff and ast-grep as programs, reads
their output into one report, and never edits code. This file routes people and AI agents to the maintained
sources.

## Start here

- Product overview, install, first run, commands: README.md
- AI-assisted explanation, install and use: AI_START_HERE.md
- Documentation index: docs/README.md
- Changes by version: CHANGELOG.md

## Reference

- The rule file, temperare.toml, every key, the baseline sets and [[override]]: docs/reference/RULE_FILE.md
- Text output, JSON output, exit codes, the next line: docs/reference/OUTPUT.md
- Each engine: the exact command line, what check means, not available and failed: docs/reference/ENGINES.md

## Policy

- What Temperare runs, what the rule file can make it do, how to report a vulnerability: SECURITY.md
- Layout of the code, build and test commands, what a change must keep: CONTRIBUTING.md
- License: MIT, in LICENSE.

## Facts an agent needs before running it

- Commands: tm check, tm rules, tm baseline test, tm install, tm uninstall, tm help, tm --version.
- tm check [--rules <path>] [--base <rev>] [--kind quality|security] [--json] [<path>...]
- tm rules [--rules <path>] [--json]
- tm baseline test [--set <name@version>] [--json]: tests each rule of a baseline set built into tm (standard@1
  unless --set names another) on its failing case (exactly the expected finding) and its passing case (no
  finding), each in a throwaway git repository. A rule holds, is broken, not available or not applicable. Exits 0
  all hold; 1 a rule is broken; 2 used wrongly, an unknown set, or a set that is not ready (--set house@1); 3
  nothing broke but a rule was not available or not applicable.
- The rule file is --rules <path>, else temperare.toml at the top of the git repository.
- Baseline sets are rules built into tm. A rule file takes one with the top-level key
  baseline = ["name@version", ...], each set once. standard@1 is ready: 53 rules, all kind quality and severity
  warning, in this order: dead code (5), deprecated calls (1), suppressions written in the code (11), then
  complexity, nesting, dbg! and print, bare and blind except and commented-out code (8), then what a change adds
  (28, each only_with_base: under not_applicable without --base). house@1 (36 rules) is not ready: a rule file that
  takes it has a problem, exit 2 ("house@1 is not ready in this build: its rules are not yet proven", fix "remove
  house@1 from baseline"), and tm baseline test --set house@1 is refused with the same two texts.
- A set's rules come first, in baseline order and each set's own order, then the file's own. tm rules lists them
  that way; nothing names a rule's set. A set rule's id starts with tm-, and an own rule's id may not.
- [[override]] changes one set rule: rule (its id, required) and any of severity, off = true (the rule is left out:
  not run, not listed), paths, exclude (each in place of the set's) and params (laid over the set's, key by key). One
  [[override]] per rule; one that names no rule of a taken set is a problem. An [[exception]] may name a set rule.
- A set rule can require params (none of standard@1 does). Until an [[override]] gives each one in its params the
  rule is not run, tm rules does not list it, and tm check lists it under not_applicable ("required params not
  given: <names>; give them in the params of an [[override]] for "<rule id>"").
- A set's ast-grep rules carry their YAML inside tm: their check is not a path in the repository and no file is
  read for it.
- The rules of a set: tm rules on a rule file that takes it, or crates/rules/baseline/<name>/<version>/set.toml.
- --json prints one JSON object on one line on stdout, with exit and next beside the result.
- tm install [--no-place] [--short-name] [--target claude,codex,cursor] [--mode skill] [--location local] [-y]
- tm install copies the binary to ~/.local/bin/temperare, links tm beside it, writes a skill file for the harnesses
  chosen, and records what it placed in ~/.local/state/temperare/installed. tm uninstall removes what that record
  names. Both exit 0 when done, 1 when a step failed, 2 when used wrongly.
- Exit codes of tm check: 0 nothing to refuse; 1 a quality error was found; 2 used wrongly or the rule file has a
  problem, nothing checked; 3 a rule was not available; 4 the only errors are security findings, which never
  refuse; 5 a rule failed. The first of 2, 1, 5, 3, 4 that applies wins.
- Exit 0 and exit 4 mean every rule ran, covered no file, or is listed under not_applicable. Exit 1 does not: read
  counts.not_available and counts.failed.
- A rule that covers none of the files git lists in the rule file's folder (tracked files in the work tree, and
  untracked files git does not ignore) runs nothing, and whether its engine is installed does not change its result
  (the engine is still asked its version for the engines list). The report does not say so:
  no line, no list entry and no count says it, and the exit code is what it would be without that rule, whether or
  not its engine is installed. So exit 0 does not say every rule had a file to check.
- --base <rev> keeps only findings on lines added since that commit. A rule with only_with_base = true reports only
  what a change adds: without --base it reports nothing and is listed under not_applicable ("reports only what a
  change adds; run with --base"). not_applicable is never a finding and never "not available".
- Exit 3 and exit 5 are never clean: the code was not fully checked.
- A rule fails (exit 5) when its engine gives no answer that can be read, or when its check cannot be matched back
  to findings: a clippy lint group, SwiftLint's custom_rules, a ruff rule name in place of a code, an ast-grep rule
  file outside the rule file's folder, a shellcheck check that is not one code, a git check other than test_ratio.
  It fails too on a param its engine does not take, or a bad value: clippy
  takes allow, and max_nesting (1-1000) with check clippy::excessive_nesting; swiftlint takes max_complexity
  (1-1000) with check cyclomatic_complexity, or max_lines (1-100000) with check file_length; ruff takes
  max_complexity (1-1000) with check C901; ast-grep takes the names its YAML has as {{name}}, and count
  ("setup-vs-tests") with shared_setup (a list of globs); git takes max_ratio (0.1-100), floor (0-100000) and
  test_paths (a list of globs), all three required; shellcheck and tessera take none. A threshold wins
  over the rule's config, and no config file of the repository is changed. The reason is in failed[].stderr_tail.
- A rule tm can refuse from the rule file alone fails whether or not its engine is installed: every check and param
  above, except the clippy lint group, an ast-grep rule file that is missing or outside the folder, and ast-grep's
  {{name}} params, which are refused only in the run. The order a rule settles in: refused, then covers no file,
  then not available, then the run (docs/reference/ENGINES.md).
- A check the installed clippy, swiftlint or ruff does not know (a misspelt name, or one newer than the engine) is
  not available (exit 3), with a why naming the engine, its version and the check.
- check, by engine: clippy, one lint or warnings; swiftlint, one rule identifier; ruff, a rule code, a code prefix,
  ALL, or several joined by commas; ast-grep, the path of a rule file inside the rule file's folder; shellcheck, one
  code such as SC2086; git, test_ratio.
- A clippy rule needs cargo-clippy and clippy-driver on PATH.
- Every finding's path is relative to the rule file's folder.
- A finding has: rule, engine, kind, severity, owner (when the rule file names one), path, line, col (when the
  engine gives one), what (the engine's message), fix (the rule's fix text).
- An exception is an [[exception]] table in the rule file with rule, path, reason and approved. It records a
  person's approval. An agent does not add one on its own.

## What it does not do

- It does not parse code, fix code or format code.
- It does not decide what a finding blocks.
- It does not install the engines.
- A check reads nothing back between runs; it only appends a line to its savings log
  (~/.local/state/temperare/savings.jsonl). Temperare has no network code of its own. The engines it runs are
  separate programs.
- When an engine ran, tm check's text output opens with an estimate of the tokens saved against the engines' raw
  output, ending in an ask to the agent to tell the user the turn's total; --json carries it as "saved", and
  savings_line = false in ~/.config/temperare/config.toml turns the line off.
- Rules with engine = "tessera" are accepted and, when they cover a file and have no params, are reported "not
  available" today, whether or not Tessera is installed. A Tessera rule with a param fails (exit 5).
- Rules with engine = "golangci-lint", "pylint", "clang-tidy" or "oclint" are accepted and, when they cover a file,
  reported "not available" (no adapter for <engine> in this build) until each adapter lands, whether or not the
  engine is installed.
- Rules with engine = "shellcheck" are not available in this build. A rule's code is looked up in a list of
  ShellCheck codes built into tm, and that list holds no code: a rule with a well-formed code and a shell script to
  check is "not available" even with ShellCheck installed (<check> is not in temperare's list of shellcheck codes),
  and ShellCheck is not run. A rule that covers no shell script runs nothing, and the report does not say so.
- Rules with engine = "git" (check test_ratio), and ast-grep rules with params.count, count what a change adds
  against a base commit. In this build tm check does not hand the base to the engines, so such a rule is "not
  available" ("reports only what a change adds; run with --base"), with or without --base.
- Any of these with only_with_base = true, run without --base, is listed under not_applicable instead, as any such
  rule is.

## Version note

This is version 0.1.0, built from source. There are no release downloads. It is built and accepted on macOS; Linux
and Windows are untested.
